title: Scar-related monomorphic ventricular tachycardia
summary: A circuit round old infarct scar sends an impulse into the ventricle with every lap.
source: Slides 77-79 (monomorphic VT; ischaemic heart disease, prior myocardial infarction)

events.label: Scar
events.caption: Old infarct scar does not conduct, but strands of surviving muscle form a slow channel through it. The circuit around the scar is drawn schematically.
events.ecg: The sinus P waves carry on at their own rate.

events.label: Slow channel
events.caption: The impulse crawls through the protected channel and exits into normal muscle at the edge of the scar.
events.ecg: The trace is flat while the impulse is inside the scar.

events.label: Ventricular activation
events.caption: From the exit site the impulse spreads through ordinary ventricular muscle, slowly and without the Purkinje system, so activation is long.
events.ecg: A wide QRS: the ventricle is activated cell to cell.

events.label: Next lap
events.caption: The circuit has gone round again and sends another impulse into the ventricle. Every lap looks the same, so the QRS complexes are identical: monomorphic VT.
events.ecg: A regular wide-complex tachycardia with identical complexes, about 175 per minute.

events.label: Atria dissociated
events.caption: The atria continue in sinus rhythm and are not related to the ventricles (AV dissociation).
events.ecg: P waves appear at a different rate from the QRS complexes, sometimes inside them.

teaching_points: Most monomorphic VT in ischaemic heart disease is scar-related reentry around an old infarct (slide 78).
A wide-complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise; AV dissociation supports the diagnosis (slides 94-97).
The slow channel through the scar is the target of catheter ablation.
